newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks to play down Gingrich China comments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks to play down Gingrich China comments.

text.p: The White House on Monday sought to play down House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich's tough talk on China and to deflect suggestions that the Republican's hard-line stance overshadowed Vice President Al Gore's visit to Beijing.

During a visit to China over the past three days, Gingrich was quoted as having told Chinese officials the United States would defend Taiwan from a mainland attack and, in public, he bluntly criticized China for its human rights record.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters at his daily briefing Gingrich was "speaking for himself" and, when asked to elaborate on U.S. policy toward any Chinese attack on Taiwan, repeatedly referred reporters to the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979, which does not commit Washington to defend the island Beijing regards as a renegade province.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, speaking at the United Nations in New York, also echoed the act's key language, saying any such attack would be of "grave concern" to the United States.

Although the act says the United States would provide Taiwan with defense materiel and services to maintain "a sufficient self-defense capability," U.S. officials said it stops short of any U.S. commitment to the island's defense.

Its language makes it U.S. policy to "consider any effort to determine the future of Taiwan by other than peaceful means a threat to the peace and security of the Western Pacific area and of grave concern to the United States."

McCurry was also acutely sensitive to suggestions that Gingrich's blunt messages to the Chinese -- in his remarks and in his risking Chinese disapproval by planning to visit Taiwan -- had cast Gore's more cautious visit in a poor light.

"He (Gore) was there to further and deepen a dialogue that we have that ultimately leads to an exchange of visits between the two presidents, and he did that exceedingly well. Mission accomplished," McCurry said.

McCurry also sought to deflect suggestions that Gore was not as tough with the Chinese on the subject of human rights, saying he had addressed the matter in a public speech and had given Chinese officials the names of dissidents the United States would like to see action on.

"He (Gore) gave exactly that speech, but my impression is that those covering his trip were covering another aspect of his trip," McCurry said. "He took a political press corps with him that covered him like he was making a trip to Des Moines instead of a trip to Beijing."
Gore visited China for four days last week, seeking to pave the way to a planned exchange of presidential visits and also to raise his own profile by undertaking a key diplomatic mission.
The vice president is widely expected to run for the White House in 2000 and has been taking a greater public role since Clinton's second term began this year.
